```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(onet2r)
library(dplyr)
helper_paths <- c(
  system.file("vignette-helpers.R", package = "onet2r"),
  "inst/vignette-helpers.R", "../inst/vignette-helpers.R"
)
helper_path <- helper_paths[nzchar(helper_paths) & file.exists(helper_paths)]
if (!length(helper_path)) stop("Could not find vignette-helpers.R.", call. = FALSE)
source(helper_path[[1]])
source(onet2r_inst_path("article-helpers", "occupational-distinctiveness.R"))
source(onet2r_inst_path("article-helpers", "software-figures.R"))
read_software <- function(name) {
  tibble::as_tibble(utils::read.csv(
    snapshot_csv_path(file.path(
      onet2r_inst_path("extdata", "occupational-software"), paste0(name, ".csv")
    )),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}
software_prevalence <- read_software("prevalence")
software_occupations <- read_software("occupations")
software_resolution <- read_software("resolution")
software_pairs <- read_software("selected-pairs")
software_provenance <- read_software("provenance")
software_diagnostics <- read_software("diagnostics")
software_identity <- read_software("identity-information")
software_sensitivity <- read_software("representation-sensitivity")
software_plots <- software_figures(
  software_prevalence, software_occupations, software_resolution, software_pairs
)
```

An accountant and a nurse might both have Excel on their software lists. That
does not make their jobs alike. But the rest of each list might tell us
something useful about how their work differs.

The [activity article](occupational-distinctiveness.html)
looks at what occupations are described as doing. This one looks at the
software examples attached to them. We keep those questions separate, then
ask whether they point to the same occupational neighbors.

These are listed examples in O&#42;NET, not observations of which programs
individual workers open.
A missing example does not prove that nobody in an occupation uses it.
Employment weights can tell us how much employment is associated with the
mapped descriptions. They cannot turn a software list into a usage survey.

## Start with something familiar

The frozen O&#42;NET 30.3 archive lists Microsoft Excel for
`r software_prevalence$n_occupations[[1]]` of the
`r software_provenance$n_occupations` covered occupations,
or `r round(100 * software_prevalence$prevalence[[1]], 1)` percent.
Word, Outlook, and PowerPoint also appear widely.

The denominator counts published data-level occupation codes. It is smaller
than the 1,016 titles in the full occupation lookup, which also contains
non-data-level entries. Some broad descriptions coexist with named
specialties. Counting these codes equally is useful for comparing records,
but does not make them disjoint groups of workers.

```{r software-common, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The eight software examples listed for the largest shares of the 923 covered occupations. Each occupation counts once per exact example string.", fig.alt = "Horizontal bars show Microsoft Excel listed for 859 of 923 occupations, 93.1 percent. Microsoft Office software follows at 88.5 percent and Microsoft Word at 84.9 percent. The table below provides all eight values."}
software_plots$common
```

```{r software-common-table, echo = FALSE}
software_prevalence |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  select(item, n_occupations, prevalence) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Listed software example", "Occupation codes", "Share of covered codes"
  ))
```

This already looks different from the detailed work activities. The most
common DWA appears in fewer than one in ten covered occupations.
The software list contains shared office programs alongside very specific
applications. The two vocabularies were built at different levels of detail,
so their prevalence numbers should not be read as a contest over which part
of work is more general.

## Rare names are easy to find

There are `r format(software_provenance$n_examples, big.mark = ",")` distinct
exact example strings. Of those,
`r format(software_provenance$n_singleton_examples, big.mark = ",")` appear in
only one covered occupation. A rarity calculation will notice those names.
Whether that is useful depends on the question.

We use the same transparent baseline as the activity article. Each occupation
gets one vote. An example's inverse document frequency is
`log(number of occupations / number listing the example)`.
An occupation's rarity summary is the mean of those values across its list.
This makes Excel contribute little and a singleton contribute much more.
These IDFs use natural logarithms. The information budget later uses bits.

It does not make the singleton more valuable, harder to learn, or more
important to a worker's day.

```{r software-inventory, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Software rarity and inventory length for all 923 covered occupations. The relationship is descriptive and may reflect how the example lists were compiled.", fig.alt = "Scatter plot of the number of listed software examples against mean inverse-prevalence rarity. Lists range from one to 430 examples. Inventory length and rarity have a positive Spearman correlation of about 0.55. No point is an estimate of job complexity."}
software_plots$size
```

```{r software-inventory-table, echo = FALSE}
software_occupations |>
  mutate(size_band = cut(
    n_examples, c(0, 10, 30, 100, Inf),
    labels = c("1 to 10", "11 to 30", "31 to 100", "101 or more")
  )) |>
  summarise(
    occupations = n(), median_rarity = median(mean_idf),
    minimum_rarity = min(mean_idf), maximum_rarity = max(mean_idf),
    .by = "size_band"
  ) |>
  arrange(size_band) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Listed examples", "Occupation codes", "Median rarity",
    "Minimum rarity", "Maximum rarity"
  ))
```

List length is worth watching. It ranges from
`r software_provenance$min_inventory` to
`r software_provenance$max_inventory` examples, and its rank correlation with
rarity is `r round(software_diagnostics$inventory_rarity_spearman, 2)`.
Here, longer lists tend to contain more unusual names too. That is the
opposite direction from the activity snapshot's inventory-size relationship.
A list is partly a record of what has been documented, so neither direction
settles how broad or specialized the underlying job is.

Three occupations tie at the maximum possible mean IDF in this snapshot:
Reinforcing Iron and Rebar Workers, Roof Bolters in Mining, and Musical
Instrument Repairers and Tuners. Every example on each of their lists is a
singleton. Their lists have four, two, and ten examples, respectively.
Each is equally distant from every other occupation under the binary
total-variation rule. Calling one neighbor the "closest" would hide a
922-way tie.

## Similarity needs more than a shared spreadsheet

Software Developers and Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers share
379 listed examples. Their lists contain 430 and 429 examples, respectively.
Registered Nurses and Licensed Practical
and Licensed Vocational Nurses share 18 examples, from lists of 43 and 26.
There is overlap, but the longer list also contains many examples that the
shorter one does not.

```{r software-pair-table, echo = FALSE}
software_pairs |>
  transmute(
    `Occupation A` = title_a, `Occupation B` = title_b,
    `Examples A` = n_a, `Examples B` = n_b,
    `Shared examples` = shared, `Profile distance` = distance
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The distance is total variation between equally weighted example lists.
For list sizes \(a\) and \(b\) sharing \(c\) examples, it is
\(1-c/\max(a,b)\). It is zero for identical lists and one for disjoint
lists. The larger inventory affects the result even when the smaller list
is entirely contained in it.

Changing the distance changes some neighbors. With five-neighbor sets
(including ties), total variation and Jaccard have a median set overlap of
`r round(median(software_sensitivity$neighbor_jaccard[software_sensitivity$comparison == "Exact-name TV versus exact-name Jaccard" & software_sensitivity$k == 5L]), 2)`.
Here overlap means shared neighbors divided by the size of their union.
Jaccard uses the union of example lists as its denominator, whereas total
variation compares their normalized shares. Neither is the uniquely correct
answer to every similarity question.

These comparisons describe software examples. They do not establish that a
developer can move easily into testing, or that the difference between nursing
roles is mostly software.

### Is the shorter list mostly inside the longer one?

A useful distinction comes from ecology. Two places can differ because they
contain different species, or because one contains a subset of the other's
species. The same set arithmetic helps with software lists, without assuming
that a missing software link means non-use.

For the nursing pair, 18 of the 26 examples on the shorter list also appear
on the longer one. For the developers and testers, 379 of 429 do.
Those fractions tell us something that a distance alone leaves out.

```{r software-components, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Selected software-list comparisons using the Sorensen decomposition. This is a different total from the total-variation distance used for the primary neighbors.", fig.alt = "Stacked horizontal bars separate replacement and nestedness-resultant dissimilarity. Accountants versus bookkeeping clerks has a total of 0.50, divided almost equally between the two components. Industrial versus graphic designers has a total of 0.57, mostly replacement. The table gives exact components for all four pairs."}
software_plots$components
```

```{r software-containment, echo = FALSE}
software_pairs |>
  transmute(
    Pair = c("Accountants / bookkeeping clerks", "Developers / testers",
             "Industrial / graphic designers", "Registered / practical nurses"),
    `Shorter list shared (%)` = 100 * shared / pmin(n_a, n_b),
    Replacement = replacement_component,
    `Nestedness-resultant` = nestedness_resultant_component,
    `Sorensen total` = sorensen_total
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 1, 3, 3, 3))
```

The last three columns use
[Baselga's pairwise decomposition](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2009.00490.x).
If \(s\) examples are shared and \(u,v\) occur in only one list, the total is
\((u+v)/(2s+u+v)\). The replacement component is
\(\min(u,v)/(s+\min(u,v))\), and the remainder is called
nestedness-resultant dissimilarity. The components add to the Sorensen total,
not to the total-variation distance above.

The terminology needs care. Replacement here means different listed examples,
not programs being replaced over time. The remainder depends on shared items
as well as list sizes. It is zero for disjoint lists, even if their sizes
differ. Neither component tells us why the lists were documented differently.
We use them to explain selected pairs and keep the original neighbor rankings.

The accountants/bookkeeping pair has a total of about 0.50, split almost
equally between the two components. The industrial/graphic-design pair has
a somewhat larger total, about 0.57, mostly from different examples.
Those are different explanations of a list difference, even though the
totals are fairly close.

## Broader labels keep some distinctions and lose others

We can group the examples into O&#42;NET's software categories and then into
broader families. Before doing that, we need to settle what an item is.

There are 151 exact example strings assigned to more than one category
somewhere in the archive. In this release, none has multiple category rows
within the same occupation. The ambiguity is across occupations.
Choosing one global category for each name would overwrite those published
assignments.

For this section only, the fine item is an **example-category pair**.
There are 8,908 such labels rather than 8,753 names. We draw an occupation
uniformly, then draw one of its listed pairs uniformly. Every pair has one
recorded category and one broader parent. Grouping keeps the original mass.
This is a separate accounting experiment from the exact-name prevalence
analysis above.

The name-only draw carries
`r sprintf("%.3f", software_identity$name_information_bits)` bits.
Keeping each name's category annotation adds
`r sprintf("%.3f", software_identity$category_annotation_bits)` bits.
That small difference is recorded separately so the classification annotation
does not get mistaken for extra detail in the software names themselves.

```{r software-resolution, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Occupation-identifying information in a fixed draw from listed example-category pairs, their 134 software categories, and their 17 broader families. Percentages use fine-pair information as the denominator.", fig.alt = "Three bars show 5.06 bits for 8,908 example-category labels, 2.20 bits for 134 categories, and 0.95 bits for 17 broader families. The broad families retain 18.7 percent of the fine-label information under this synthetic draw."}
software_plots$resolution
```

```{r software-resolution-table, echo = FALSE}
software_resolution |>
  mutate(grain = c("Example-category pair", "Software category", "Broader family")) |>
  select(grain, n_labels, information_bits, retained_percent) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Vocabulary", "Labels", "Information (bits)", "Fine-label information retained (%)"
  ))
```

Broader families retain about
`r round(software_resolution$retained_percent[[3]], 1)` percent of the
fine-label information about occupation identity under this draw.
Some loss is guaranteed when labels are grouped. The amount tells us what
this particular classification discards, not whether broader categories are
bad. "Database software" may be exactly the level we need for one question
and too broad for another.

Re-counting every category as simply present or absent would answer a
different question. It is useful for category prevalence, but it is not
the same mass-preserving calculation.

The binary category view also changes the neighbors. At five neighbors, its
median set overlap with the exact-name comparison is
`r round(median(software_sensitivity$neighbor_jaccard[software_sensitivity$comparison == "Exact-name TV versus category-presence TV" & software_sensitivity$k == 5L]), 2)`.
The bundled sensitivity table includes one-, five-, and ten-neighbor sets,
with cutoff ties retained. A result about "similar software" needs to say
which of these resolutions and distances it uses.

## What these lists leave open

We preserve exact spelling as the baseline. Lowercasing and trimming repeated
or surrounding whitespace change neither the number of distinct names nor
the number of links in this snapshot. That check does not resolve product
aliases, renamed applications, or the overlap between a software suite and
its individual programs. Those would need a reviewed crosswalk.

The Hot Technology and In Demand flags are also different from usage.
The former concerns requirements appearing frequently across employer job
postings. The latter concerns postings for the particular occupation.
Neither is a numeric estimate of how frequently workers use a program.

The practical next question is whether these software neighbors agree with
neighbors based on activities and required skills. The
[companion activity article](occupational-distinctiveness.html) makes that
comparison on common occupation codes and keeps the distances separate.
An overlap is a similarity between records. A disagreement is a useful
pair to inspect, not proof that one domain has found the "real" occupation.

## Reproduce the snapshot

Article builds read bundled derived tables and make no network requests.
The package does not export a software-distinctiveness score.
To regenerate the tables from the pinned public ZIP, run from the repository:

```{r software-reproduction, eval = FALSE}
# Download the public 30.3 text archive separately, then:
# Rscript data-raw/occupational-software.R path/to/db_30_3_text.zip
```

The script checks the archive's SHA-256, audits item identity, and writes the
prevalence, occupation summaries, neighbors, selected pairs, coverage,
resolution, and provenance tables. The full-archive snapshot is separate
from the small stylized fixtures used to test the formulas.
The largest tables are losslessly compressed as `.csv.gz`; base R's
`read.csv()` reads those files directly.

This article derives information from the O&#42;NET 30.3 Database by the
U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA),
under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
O&#42;NET is a trademark of USDOL/ETA. The prevalence, distances and
information calculations are modifications by onet2r, not approved,
endorsed or tested by USDOL/ETA.
